briefs.headline: 'Naman Dhir has finished him': World Cup winner's big statement on star's T20I future
briefs.deck: Naman Dhir had scored 318 runs in IPL 2026 but did not bowl a single over during the tournament. His international debut showed that he can offer India another option with the ball. Former India cricketer and 1983 World Cup winner Krishnamachari Srikkanth believes Dhir’s emergence could seriously hurt Washington Sundar’s chances in white-ball cricket.
briefs.bodyText:
Naman Dhir made a strong statement on his T20I debut against the West Indies, and his performance has already led to questions about 
Washington Sundar
’s place in India’s white-ball teams.
The 25-year-old, who has mainly been seen as a batting all-rounder in the IPL, surprised many with the ball in the first T20I. He bowled his full four-over spell and returned figures of 3/31 as India restricted the West Indies to 171.
Dhir had scored 318 runs in IPL 2026 but did not bowl a single over during the tournament. His international debut showed that he can offer India another option with the ball.
Former India cricketer and 1983 World Cup winner Krishnamachari Srikkanth believes Dhir’s emergence could seriously hurt Washington Sundar’s chances in white-ball cricket.
Srikkanth: 'Naman Dhir has finished him'
Srikkanth pointed out that Dhir initially came into the team as a replacement but has now made it difficult for the selectors to leave him out.
"Naman Dhir has now come in at Washington Sundar's place as a replacement player. Washington Sundar keeps getting injured after every two matches. Now Naman Dhir has come in as his replacement and finished him. How can you drop Naman Dhir now from ODIs and T20Is? He has immediately grabbed that spot. 
Now Washington Sundar can only play for India in Test cricket," Srikkanth said on his YouTube channel.
Srikkanth was also impressed by how Dhir adjusted his bowling after getting hit.
"When he bowls fast, he gets hit for sixes. So he immediately slows the ball down, which shows that he's a very thoughtful bowler. He's ideal for T20 cricket. He bowls in such a way that he envisions himself batting and how one would bowl to him. That's how much of a thinking cricketer he looks to be. That's why he's an intelligent bowler."
Why Srikkanth wants Impact Player rule removed
Dhir’s performance also made Srikkanth question the impact of the IPL’s Impact Player rule.
"This is why the Impact Player rule should be removed in the IPL. That's how you'll produce genuine all-rounders. Now you've got a good batting all-rounder in Naman Dhir. Today he bowled four overs, but even if he gives you two overs on a consistent basis, it'll be huge for India and MI," said Srikkanth.
Srikkanth expects Dhir to get more opportunities with the ball in the IPL as well.
"He'll take loads of wickets even in the upcoming IPL. He must have bowled only 10 overs maximum in his IPL career, yet he bowled four overs today. He has everything, including luck."
Dhir says bowling has always been part of his game
Dhir, however, made it clear that his bowling was not something he suddenly picked up for his international debut.
“I have been bowling for quite some time; it is not as if I have just started now. In the IPL, because of the impact-player rule, you don’t see me bowling as much. But it is not that I haven’t bowled. I have bowled a lot and have good experience here as well. Hopefully, I will continue doing well in the future,” Dhir said in the post-match press conference after helping India bowl out West Indies for 171 in the first T20I here.
He explained that he followed a simple plan after watching Axar Patel bowl earlier in the innings.
“I saw Axar Bhai bowling earlier, and he was bowling a little slower and getting some turn. That was in my mind - if I bowled a little slower, there would be good grip from the wicket, and I could get them out. So I just stuck to my plans and kept things basic. I think I got a good result from that," Dhir said.
'I am working just as hard on my bowling'
Dhir also stressed that his bowling has always received the same attention as his batting.
“Again, I will say that even if you haven’t seen me bowling, I have been bowling as much as I have since I came here and I have practised just as much before this. It is not as if, as a batting all-rounder or bowling all-rounder, I have neglected one aspect. Yes, my batting is a plus point, but at the same time I am working just as hard on my bowling,” he said.
“Whether I have to bowl four overs, two overs or even one-day cricket, where I have bowled six or seven overs, it is normal for me. I just have to focus on my plans and try to execute them,” he added.
India, who won the three-match ODI series 2-1, are leading the five-match T20I series 1-0.

briefs.headline: The journey from a promising partnership to a world-class combination for Manush and Diya
briefs.deck: For Indian table tennis, it was the fourth medal at the Asian Games and ensured that the sport had a podium finish for a third consecutive time
briefs.bodyText:
For four days in early September, Manush Shah travelled to Mumbai, the hometown of his mixed doubles partner Diya Chitale for a relatively simple job. Train.
There were no selection meetings to worry about, no administrative developments to follow, no uncertainty over who would be around the Indian table tennis team. In Mumbai, the pair could concentrate on the one thing that had brought them together in the first place — making their partnership work.
Those four days would prove valuable when they eventually arrived in Aichi-Nagoya.
The sixth-seeded Indian pair went on to win a bronze medal at the Asian Games, beating Hong Kong’s third-seeded Wong Chun Ting and Doo Hoi Kem in the quarterfinals before losing to eventual silver medallists Wong Chuqin and Sun Yingsha of China in the semifinals.
For Indian table tennis, the medal was significant. It was the fourth at the Asian Games and ensured that the sport had a podium finish at a third successive edition of the continental extravaganza.
For Manush and Diya, though, the bronze represented something more personal. It was the reward for a partnership that had steadily climbed the international ladder and, in the process, had learnt to complement two very different games.
It was also an affirmation that, amid a turbulent build-up, they had managed to keep the noise away from the table.
When Diya spoke about going into her second Asian Games, she did not need to be reminded of the difference between a regular international tournament and a multi-sport event. Her first Asian Games, in Hangzhou three years ago, had given her that perspective.
“Going into my second Asian Games, I think the first one gave me a lot of experience and exposure,” Diya told The Hindu before leaving for Japan. “Representing the country at a multi-sport event is a very different feeling. It was a great experience in 2023, and I wanted to carry that experience forward.” But there was a difference this time. The expectations were higher. Diya and Manush were no longer simply an emerging combination hoping to make an impression. They had become one of India’s principal medal contenders, their progress reflected by a place among the world’s top-eight pairs at the 2025 WTT Finals, the season-ending event reserved for the leading performers of the year.
“We have been doing really well in doubles,” Diya had said ahead of the Games. “Me and Manush have been doing really, really well for the last two or three years. When we started, our graph has gone up a lot.”
That graph eventually took them to an Asian Games podium. The bronze did not arrive out of nowhere. Over the preceding seasons, the pair had learnt the demands of international mixed doubles, where the rhythm and speed of a rally can differ considerably from men’s doubles.
Manush described the distinction in simple terms. “In men’s doubles, you expect power from the opponents. The ball really travels and you expect good quality, so you don’t have to manage the front-and-back movement as much,” he said.
“In mixed doubles, it is the opposite. The front-and-back movement becomes really important because the woman on the opposing pair may not be as powerful. They try to play quickly, so the ball can be a little slower and you have to make faster adjustments with your footwork.” That difference requires more than just technical ability. It requires trust. “In mixed doubles, Diya is the one with the control and I try to finish the point,” Manush said. “If this works out, then we are already one step ahead of the opponent. That is what the goal is all about in doubles.” The quarterfinal against Hong Kong was evidence of that equation working when it mattered.
India’s table tennis contingent had not arrived at Aichi-Nagoya without precedent. In 2018, the men’s team won a historic bronze and Sharath Kamal and Manika Batra added another bronze in mixed doubles. In Hangzhou, Ayhika Mukherjee and Sutirtha Mukherjee produced a surprise run to the women’s doubles bronze. Manush and Diya’s medal therefore extended the sequence of Indian table tennis appearing on the Asian Games podium. Yet it carried a different weight.
Unlike the Hangzhou women’s doubles bronze, which came as a surprise, this was a medal India had begun to expect from the pair. Their qualification for the WTT Finals in 2025 had placed them among the world’s leading combinations, while their performances over the preceding couple of seasons had made them a credible medal proposition.
“Since two or three years, we have been doing really well,” Diya had said. “We understand each other’s game better now. We know each other’s strengths and weaknesses.”
That understanding had been tested against the world’s best. “We have played a lot of top pairs over the years,” she said. “We have beaten a top Japanese pair and qualified for the WTT Finals, where the top eight pairs in the world play. All these experiences put together have helped us reach where we are today.”
The Asian Games simply provided the biggest stage yet on which that accumulated experience had to translate into a result. And it did. The achievement becomes more significant when the build-up to the Asian Games is considered. Indian table tennis spent much of the preceding months dealing with issues away from the playing arena.
The selection controversy surrounding Manika Batra had cast a shadow over the process after she was left out of the Asian Games squad for failing to meet the prescribed selection criteria. The episode led to questions about the transparency of the selection system and public exchanges between the paddler and the federation.
Then, in August, the Sports Ministry suspended the recognition of the Table Tennis Federation of India as the National Sports Federation for table tennis, citing a series of administrative and governance issues. The turmoil had consequences beyond the boardroom.
Massimo Costantini’s tenure as India’s foreign expert had expired on May 15, and the uncertainty surrounding the federation meant his continuation with the national set-up was delayed. The Italian eventually joined the Indian contingent in Japan only a week before the Asian Games. Against that backdrop, Manush and Diya had little choice but to concentrate on what they could control.
Rising expectations
There was no luxury of an extended camp dedicated exclusively to the mixed doubles combination. The international calendar rarely allows it. But the partnership had already developed enough understanding to make those sessions count.
Diya was aware before the Games that expectations would follow them. The pair’s rise had ensured that. “Pressure is always going to be there,” she had said. “There will always be some expectations and some pressure. But what is important is that we gave our best and are happy with the way it progressed.” That attitude became particularly relevant in the quarterfinal. A defeat would have meant another near-miss for Indian table tennis. A victory would guarantee at least a bronze. Manush and Diya delivered. The win over Wong and Doo, seeded third, confirmed the medal and effectively transformed their status from contenders to medallists. The bronze was secure.
While Manush has come a long way since starting to train under Shailesh Gosain’s watchful eyes in Vadodara, Diya has been coached by Sachin Shetty ever since she took up the sport more than a decade and a half ago. Since their junior days, Olympic Gold Quest has been supporting the duo’s journey towards excellence in the international circuit. Government support has also reduced some of the financial pressure on athletes and their families. “With so many government schemes, the Government helps a lot with the TOPS scheme,” Diya said. “Of course, that also relieves the financial pressure on the parents.” That support becomes especially relevant when an athlete is required to travel extensively, train continuously and compete against the world’s best.
By the time Diya and Manush stepped onto the Asian Games arena, they were carrying the work of that entire ecosystem with them. More than just a bronze. The significance of the medal extends beyond the result of one quarterfinal and one semifinal.
It means India has now won table tennis medals at three consecutive Asian Games. It means the country has a established mixed doubles combination capable of competing with the best in Asia. And it confirms that Manush and Diya’s journey from promising partnership to world-class combination has been real. Their qualification for the 2025 WTT Finals had already indicated where they belonged. The Asian Games provided a different kind of test — one where the draw, the occasion and the weight of expectations all mattered.
They responded by beating the third seeds and securing India’s only table tennis medal at the Games. The loss to the Chinese pair in the semifinal did not diminish what had been achieved. If anything, it reinforced the progression.
Three years earlier, Diya had entered her first Asian Games looking for experience and exposure while Manush had endured the disappointment of being one point away from a medal in men’s doubles. This time they went for a medal.
“We went into the Asian Games aiming for a medal,” Diya said. “And we are thrilled that we have achieved the objective and have brought that medal home”.

briefs.headline: ‘Nobody can stop Bumrah & Bhuvi’: Ashwin’s bold prediction as pacer makes India return
briefs.deck: Ravichandran Ashwin asserts that Bhuvneshwar Kumar’s display in New Zealand might have a significant impact on his chances for World Cup selection. Having last participated in an ODI in 2022, Bhuvneshwar is set to make his return to international cricket. His capacity to swing the ball could enhance India's bowling lineup for next year’s championship.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Former India spinner 
Ravichandran Ashwin
 believes 
Bhuvneshwar Kumar
’s return to international cricket could open the door for a remarkable comeback to India’s ODI squad and potentially take the veteran pacer to next year’s 50-over World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.
Bhuvneshwar, who returned to India colours after nearly four years when he was picked for the upcoming five-match T20I series in New Zealand, last played an ODI against South Africa at Paarl in 2022.
Ashwin feels the selectors will be watching Bhuvneshwar closely in New Zealand and that a successful series could immediately put him in contention for the ODI side ahead of the World Cup.
“He is going to New Zealand now. I am telling you, if he does well, everyone will immediately say, just take him for the ODI team as well. The selectors will be watching very closely,” Ashwin said on his YouTube channel.
‘Nobody can stop’ Bumrah-Bhuvneshwar combination
Ashwin went a step further, saying Bhuvneshwar’s ability to swing the ball and maintain decent pace could make him a valuable option in conditions in South Africa and Australia.
“If he swings the ball and shows decent fitness, nobody can stop 
Jasprit Bumrah
 and Bhuvneshwar Kumar from sitting together on that flight to the World Cup, with Bhuvneshwar bowling the first ball of the World Cup,” said Ashwin.
The 36-year-old seamer has played 121 ODIs and taken 141 wickets. His ability to move the ball both ways, particularly with the new ball, is a skill Ashwin believes could be particularly useful in conditions where seam and swing can play a major role.
“Do you want swing? He has swing. If you want it to move one way, he can do that. If you want it to move both ways, he can do that too. And then he has decent pace,” he added.
Bhuvneshwar’s recent performances in the IPL have also strengthened his case for an international comeback. He played a key role in Royal Challengers Bengaluru’s back-to-back IPL titles, taking 17 wickets in the 2025 season and 28 in 2026.
Ashwin highlights one major concern
While Ashwin remains bullish about Bhuvneshwar’s skill set, he stressed that fitness could be crucial if the pacer is to extend his international career and push for a place at the World Cup.
“I am once again putting my neck on the line to say this: if he had worked a little harder, if the timing had been right and if he had avoided those injuries, with the skill set he possesses, he could have been a king for India across all formats,” he said.
Apart from 21 Tests and 121 ODIs, Bhuvneshwar has played 87 T20Is and taken 90 wickets. His return also gives India another experienced seamer alongside the likes of Jasprit Bumrah, while potentially offering guidance to younger pacers such as Mayank Yadav and Prince Yadav.
India will play five T20Is against New Zealand later this month before the tour moves into the ODI and Test phases, giving Bhuvneshwar an immediate opportunity to make a case for a longer international comeback.

briefs.headline: Smriti Mandhana, India’s new captain, has earned her job
briefs.deck: The 30-year-old, who is the most experienced player in the side after Harmanpreet, has also led RCB to two WPL titles; the southpaw’s immediate task will be to strengthen the team in the shortest format
briefs.bodyText:
The queen of batting is all set for a new reign.
Smriti Mandhana, the most prolific batter in women’s cricket, has taken over the captaincy of the Indian team from Harmanpreet Kaur. She wasn’t just the obvious choice; she was the only choice.
She commands respect from her teammates. And she is the most experienced player in the team after Harmanpreet.
The 30-year-old is not new to the leadership role, either. She has stepped in when Harmanpreet wasn’t available on a few occasions. She has also led Royal Challengers Bengaluru to two WPL titles. The first of those titles, in 2024, brought an end to the agonisingly long wait for a trophy for the Bengaluru-based franchise, whose men’s team used to falter after promising much, season after season.
Smriti has an opportunity to end a title drought for the Women in Blue, too. They have never won the T20 World Cup. They didn’t even make it to the knockout stage in the last editions.
Strengthening the Indian team for the shortest format should be her priority. India is excellent in ODIs; the World Cup victory last year underlined that fact.
The Indians are pretty good in the longest format, too, though women get to play Test matches only once in a blue moon. They were ruthless against England in the historic Test at Lord’s recently. But, there is work to be done in their T20 side.
They have struggled against stronger teams like Australia and South Africa. They need to address the issue of batting firepower in the middle-order, instead of leaving everything to Richa Ghosh. They have to find, and develop, some quality all-rounders. Smriti, and the team management, will have to address those issues well in time for the next T20 World Cup in 2028.
Along with privilege, captaincy also brings in added pressure. Given her gift, ambition and fearlessness, it is unlikely to affect Smriti’s batting. Who knows, it may help, even.

briefs.headline: Out on bail after rape allegation, Porel named in Bengal squad for Ranji opener
briefs.deck: Wicketkeeper-batter Abhishek Porel has been included in Bengal's squad for their upcoming Ranji Trophy match. He was previously arrested on allegations of rape but has since been granted bail. The team has named a strong squad with senior pacers Mohammed Shami and Akash Deep included. Bengal's match against Delhi is set to take place in Kalyani to mark the season opener.
briefs.bodyText:
KOLKATA: Wicketkeeper-batter Abhishek Porel, who was recently granted bail in a case involving allegations of rape and other sexual offences, has been included in Bengal's 17-member squad for their Ranji Trophy season opener against Delhi in Kalyani.
Porel, who has not played competitive cricket since the end of IPL 2026, was arrested in August following allegations that he had sexual relations with a woman on the promise of marriage. He was subsequently granted bail and has now been picked for Bengal's Elite Group C opener, with Abhimanyu Easwaran continuing as captain.
The match will be played at the Bengal Cricket Academy Ground in Kalyani after Bengal's season opener was moved from the iconic Eden Gardens. The venue switch comes as Eden Gardens prepares to host Prime Minister Narendra Modi for the launch of the Durga Puja festivities around Mahalaya on October 10.
Abhishek Porel returns to Bengal squad
Porel's inclusion comes after he was also named in Bengal's squad for practice matches in Guwahati last month. At the time, a Cricket Association of Bengal (CAB) official told Cricinfo: "His personal and legal matters are his own matters. If the situation changes, we will take the appropriate action. 
But for now there's no issue from our side."
Porel was arrested by Mogra police in Hooghly district on August 11 following a complaint filed by a woman medical student from Karnataka. Police said the woman alleged that she had been in a relationship with Porel for around three-and-a-half years and that they had planned to get married.
Police registered a case under several provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including Section 69, along with provisions of the Information Technology Act. Hooghly (Rural) Superintendent of Police Kunwar Bhushan Singh had confirmed Porel's arrest at the time, saying, "There was a case lodged against him and a court order to arrest him. He was arrested late last night. He will be produced in court today.
"
Shami, Akash Deep bolster Bengal pace attack
Porel's inclusion apart, Bengal have named a strong pace attack for their campaign, with senior India pacer Mohammed Shami, Mukesh Kumar and Akash Deep all part of the squad. Akash Deep, who is returning from injury, will be keen to get valuable match time as he looks to regain his rhythm and fitness ahead of India's New Zealand tour.
Sudip Kumar Gharami has been named Easwaran's deputy, while Shahbaz Ahmed, who sustained an injury during the Duleep Trophy, has been left out.
Bengal finished top of their group last season before their campaign ended in the semi-finals against eventual champions Jammu and Kashmir.
Bengal and Delhi are grouped alongside Gujarat, Jharkhand, Kerala, Maharashtra, Odisha and Services.

Kaif, Soummyadip Mandal.
- Stand-bys: Karan Lal, Akhilesh Yadav, Geet Puri, Abishek Kr. Raman, Subham Sarkar, Sumit Mohanta, Aditya Purohit.

briefs.headline: Ranji Trophy: Vishnu Vinod ready to leave his imprint as Kerala captain
briefs.deck: The 32-year-old batter from Pathanamthitta, who also keeps wickets, takes charge of the Kerala team ahead of the Ranji Trophy opener against Jharkhand in Jamshedpur on October 11.
briefs.bodyText:
KOCHI: Kerala's newly appointed captain, 
Vishnu Vinod
, wants to leave his imprint on this team, but he is keen that his players feel free to express themselves and play to their potential.
The 32-year-old batter from Pathanamthitta, who also keeps wickets, takes charge of the Kerala team ahead of the 
Ranji Trophy
 opener against Jharkhand in Jamshedpur on October 11. "We are going into this season with a positive mindset, and all our energies are focused on the first game," he told TOI. "I want to leave my imprint on this team, but I also want the boys to express themselves and not worry about their spot in the squad."
The core group is the same one that reached the Ranji final two seasons ago. The big change is in the dressing room, where former Goa batter 
Swapnil Asnodkar
 is the new coach. "I played several games against him when he was playing for Goa. He's like an elder brother," Vinod said. "We're working on getting players to perform to the best of their potential."
Kerala pacer M D Nidheesh calls Vinod's elevation an aggressive move. "He's a captain who plays for results, very proactive and aggressive, with an out-of-the-box approach. He's very inventive with his field settings," Nidheesh said.
He points to Kerala's last league game of the previous season, against Goa. "On a dead, lifeless pitch, Kerala still forced an outright result, ending a lacklustre campaign on a high, thanks mainly to Vinod's captaincy," Nidheesh noted.
KCA secretary Vinod S Kumar says the game against Goa in Porvorim, in which Kerala won by 9 wickets, was what prompted the selectors to hedge their bets on Vinod.
"The team management and the selectors were impressed by how he marshalled his resources. It was a dead game for us, so we decided to give him a chance to lead, and he didn't disappoint."
Kumar says Vinod endured a lean patch a couple of seasons ago, following which he bounced back via white-ball cricket. "He was out of form, but he got his verve back after strong performances in white-ball tournaments like the Syed Mushtaq Trophy."
Kerala's squad blends youth and experience. The batting is led by Sachin Baby, Rohan S Kunnummal, Vinod, Mohammed Azharuddeen and Salman Nizar. MD Nidheesh, Eden Apple Tom and Basil N P spearhead the bowling, and veterans Jalaj Saxena and Aditya Sarwate are the guest players.
They are placed in Elite Group C with Jharkhand, Odisha, Bengal, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Delhi, and Services.

briefs.headline: ‘Changed Shreyas’ grip & backlift’: How Nayar helped India T20I captain bounce back
briefs.deck: Facing a troubling drop in performance, with no scores exceeding 30 in his last ten T20I outings, Shreyas Iyer turned to Abhishek Nayar for help. Their two-hour conversation revolved around critical adjustments to Iyer's batting style. The results were evident as Iyer responded with a stellar 102 not out in the first T20I against West Indies, underscoring his tenacity and capacity to rebound from…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Since he scored an 80 not out against England in July, India's T20I captain 
Shreyas Iyer
 had been experiencing a rare slump in white-ball cricket, where he’s usually highly consistent, having failed to cross 30 in his last 10 T20I innings.
Soon after he landed back in Mumbai after leading India to the gold medal at the 2026 Asian Games in Japan, where he was out for 13 & 21 in the semi-final and final, Shreyas, surely concerned by his dip in form, sought out his old Mumbai teammate, friend and 'mentor' Abhishek Nayar, India's former assistant coach and currently the head coach of Kolkata Knight Riders, for help.
The result: Iyer cracked a brilliant 43-ball 102 not out, including six sixes and 10 fours, to fashion India's eight-wicket triumph in the opening T20I against West Indies in Lucknow.
After his blazing knock, Iyer said in a video released by the 
BCCI
 on Tuesday that a conversation with Nayar had aided his performance. “I had a brief interaction with Abhishek Nayar in that period (during his time in Japan) where we were talking about cricket. I think that conversation with him helped me a lot in today’s performance. The key note which I observed in my batting today was setting myself before the delivery of the ball, and that worked perfectly. 
So, to create that momentum and rhythm was essential at the start of the innings, and it worked out pretty well.”
TOI has learnt that Nayar went to meet Shreyas at his home in Worli in Mumbai, and the two, who go back a long way, had a long chat about what could be wrong with his batting. Nayar revealed that for a brief while, Iyer had begun doubting his ability to smash those trademark massive sixes that normally sail into the crowd.
The productive two-hour chat session took place at Iyer's Worli home, during which Nayar ironed out a few technical things in Iyer's game. "I went to meet him and he was feeling that he wasn't getting the power to hit sixes. He wasn't feeling that he could hit a sixer. So, we spoke about some technical things and made some changes in batting. We spent two hours on his grip and backlift. I can't tell you what exactly, but I changed his grip and backlift a little bit.
 Basically, I made a slight alteration to his grip, the initial movement and his backlift," Nayar told TOI.
While churning out one stroke after another, Iyer looked back to his confident self on Monday. "There was no issue with his confidence or batting. He was missing the 'feel' to hit sixes and that was it," Nayar asserted.
It helped that over the years, Nayar has followed Iyer's batting closely. "I compared his old videos and tried to set him up to get to what is normally very comfortable with him. I did a little bit and set him up. It's such an old relationship. It's such an understanding, that it doesn't take that much time," the former India and Mumbai allrounder said.
Since resuming his role as T20I captain this year, Iyer has scored 511 runs in 17 innings at an average of 39.30 and a strike rate above 149, including one century and two fifties.

briefs.headline: Archery Premier League | All set for the second season
briefs.bodyText:
When the dust settled at the 2026 Asian Games, one sport stood taller than the rest. Archery hit the bullseye, hauling in nine medals (five gold, two silver and two bronze) and, for good measure, bringing the mighty South Koreans down a peg or two.
Then came the encore. Two quotas for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics were secured, courtesy of Chikitha Taniparthi and Sahil Jadhav in the Mixed Team Compound and Kumkum Mohod in the Women’s Individual Recurve.
The country’s finest archers have assembled once again, this time in Hyderabad to team up with international rivals and compete against their compatriots in the second season of the Archery Premier League (APL).
Chikitha, whose twin gold caught the nation’s attention in Aichi-Nagoya, credited APL for helping refine her game.
“During the first season, I learnt a lot about managing pressure under the faster shot clock as well as techniques from my teammates while watching them train. It helped a lot in me getting better as an archer and played a part in winning gold at the Asian Games,” she said at the pre-season press conference.
Interest in the league has only grown since the inaugural campaign in New Delhi, according to APL director Anil Kamineni. He revealed plans to add more teams in the future and announced that the APL caravan will pitch its tent in a new city every year.
A rematch of last season’s title clash between Rajputana Royals, the defending champion, and Prithviraaj Yodhas will get this edition underway at the People’s Plaza on Thursday.
